title: Dunkirk
events_chronological: Leaflets fall on Dunkirk and German fire drives the private soldier Tommy through the streets to the beach, the only one of his patrol to make it.
Tommy meets Gibson burying a body, and the two carry a wounded man onto a hospital ship to get themselves aboard.
They are turned back off the ship, which is bombed and sunk in the harbour behind them.
Tommy, Gibson and Alex hide in a beached trawler outside the perimeter, waiting for the tide to lift it.
German soldiers use the trawler for target practice, and the men inside argue about throwing Gibson overboard to lighten it.
The trawler floods and Gibson drowns, and the survivors swim clear into a burning oil slick.
Commander Bolton watches from the mole as ship after ship is sunk and the perimeter shrinks around the beach.
In Weymouth the civilian sailor Mr. Dawson takes his boat Moonstone out himself with his son Peter and their friend George rather than surrender her to the navy.
They pick a shivering soldier off the hull of a wrecked ship, and he panics when he learns they are heading for Dunkirk.
In the struggle George is thrown down the ladder and blinded, and he dies later in the cabin.
Three Spitfires cross the Channel; the leader is shot down almost at once and Farrier takes over with a smashed fuel gauge.
Collins is hit and ditches in the sea, and his canopy jams as the aircraft fills and sinks.
Mr. Dawson brings Moonstone alongside and Peter smashes the canopy in to pull Collins out.
Farrier shoots down the bomber attacking the minesweeper, saving the men in the water and on the mole.
Moonstone reaches the oil slick and takes Tommy, Alex and others aboard as the fuel catches fire.
Farrier, out of fuel, glides the length of the beach, brings down one more aircraft, lands past the perimeter and burns his Spitfire before he is taken prisoner.
The little ships arrive and the evacuation succeeds, and Bolton stays behind for the French.
Tommy and Alex reach England expecting contempt and are handed beer and blankets, and Tommy reads Churchill's speech aloud from a newspaper.
syuzhet_notes: The film runs three strands at three different durations - a week on the mole, a day at sea, an hour in the air - and cuts between them as though they were simultaneous, so a Spitfire ten minutes into its flight appears alongside soldiers who have been waiting for days. Told order and chronology therefore come apart continuously, and the film shows one event twice from two strands: Farrier's kill over the minesweeper is seen from the water before it is seen from the cockpit.
fabula_notes: Because the three strands cover different spans of time, putting them on one clock means deciding where the shorter ones start inside the longest, which the film fixes only at the moments the strands physically meet. The German forces are never seen, so their movements are inferred entirely from their effects.
